articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworm is spreading in the US, threatening livestock and wildlife – hunters can be the first line of defense
articles.author: Jacob Dykes, Assistant Professor of Wildlife Management, Mississippi State University
paras: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk.
The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets.
That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further.

As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab, we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations.
The problem with screwworm

Unlike other blowflies, New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk.

Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles, where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites.
Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death.
How the US eradicated screwworm in the past
All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock.
In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today.

The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas.

The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population.

Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap, Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again. Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward. There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S.
The Florida Key deer infestation

Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population: the Florida Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium).

At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals. Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key, they were monitored more closely than most wildlife.

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population, but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered.

In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico.

The number of cases in animals had passed 120 as of Nov. 7, 2026, including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas. The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading.
Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring.

Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm.
For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever.
Tapping an army of conservationists: Hunters
Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters.

According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk.

White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting.

That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help.
What to watch for as a hunter
If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals, especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds.

Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately.
As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread.

Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock.

articles.title: The Cop31 climate summit is betting on electrification – but still needs a plan to ditch fossil fuels
articles.author: Freddie Daley, Research Associate, Centre for Global Political Economy, University of Sussex
paras: The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, will get underway in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9. One of its key objectives is to boost electrification across the global economy – replacing petrol and diesel vehicles, gas boilers and some industrial processes that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives.

The summit’s host, Turkey, has set a target of 35% of energy demand being met by electricity by 2035, up from around 20% today. Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels.

Without doubt, electrification is essential to curtailing greenhouse gas emissions, and is already gathering pace. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has declared we are living in the “age of electricity”, and if stated policy pledges hold, global electrification rates will hit 31% by 2050. The Cop31’s focus on electrification hopes to build upon and accelerate this existing trend.

But electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain: the continued expansion of fossil fuel production, and growing geopolitical competition over clean technologies where the latter is increasingly shaping governments’ climate and energy policies, as they struggle to compete with dominant “electrostates” such as China.

The Australian climate minister and Cop31’s president of negotiations has described electrification and fossil fuel reduction as “different sides of the same coin”. But they are not interchangeable. Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply.

By 2030, governments are planning to produce more than double the amount of fossil fuels than would be consistent with limiting warning to 1.5°C. More concerning is that this assessment was made before the conflict and disruption in the Middle East, which has caused the US, Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada and other fossil fuel producers to increase output in the name of energy security. The UK, meanwhile, has approved the Jackdaw gasfield in a purported bid to protect jobs and keep homes warm.

The 35-by-35 target is also silent on where that additional electricity will come from. After all, a country could in theory increase its rate of electrification by burning more fossil fuels (imagine a country where every car was electric, but all that electricity came from coal).
A genuine energy transition

What’s needed is the two-pronged approach of electrifying economies while simultaneously phasing out fossil fuels and reducing their supply. This will ensure capital is reallocated to renewable energy for electrification. Governments can do this nationally or through international initiatives such as the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance, the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and the Cop-adjacent conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

Skirting the fossil fuel issue is nothing new at these summits. It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021. And even then it only passed with calls to “phasedown” unabated coal power and phase-out “inefficient” fossil fuel subsidies.

At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda. Brazil has published an extensive voluntary “roadmap” to guide governments’ phase-out efforts, but this sits outside the formal negotiations and lacks timelines.
This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels?

Even growing demand for electricity does not guarantee a clean energy transition. The data centre boom in the US and beyond, for instance, is driving the use of gas and coal to generate electricity. The International Gas Union, a lobby group for natural gas producers, is explicitly positioning gas as a way to meet growing demand from data centres and AI.

Increasing electrification looks relatively straightforward: just encourage more renewable energy production and electric vehicles. Yet, for most of the world, this would mean overcoming security and trade tensions with China, whose dominance in clean technologies, manufacturing and rare earth processing makes it a lynchpin electrostate in a world hoping to electrify everything.

China’s dominance is near total. For the component materials of solar panels, in 2024 China controlled 93% of global polysilicon processing, 97% of wafer manufacturing – making the thin slices of silicon that form the basis of solar panels – 92% of solar cell manufacturing and 86% of solar module production. It also produced more than 80% of electric vehicle batteries in 2025. According to the IEA, China is dominant across 19 of 20 energy-related strategic minerals, averaging over 70% of processing control. Achieving global electrification targets will therefore require continued access to Chinese technologies, products and raw materials.

This runs counter to almost two decades of western policy aimed at protecting domestic industries from Chinese competition and restricting China’s technological development, most notably with semi-conductors. While these efforts have largely failed to contain Chinese innovation, an overreliance on Chinese clean technologies is increasingly seen as a “serious risk” to Europe’s economic and national security. European governments have responded with tariffs and restrictions on Chinese imports and investments, while seeking to build up their own manufacturing capacity.

Governments face a difficult dilemma. Opening their economies further to Chinese technologies could mean unpicking trade protections developed over years and create new dependencies, while refusing to cooperate with China risks slowing electrification and may even drive some governments to abandon climate and energy policies altogether because they cannot compete.
While the drive towards electrification at Cop31 is to be welcomed, it cannot be a substitute for the harder political task of securing binding commitments to phase out fossil fuels, fast and fairly.

articles.title: Don’t wash your laundry at teatime – why planning energy use can reduce your bills
articles.author: Lala Rukh, PhD Candidate, Energy, University of Galway; Atlantic Technological University
paras: For decades, judging a home’s energy performance meant asking one question: how much does it use? Labels such as energy performance certificates still ask only that.

But homes are changing. Add solar panels, a battery or an electric car, and a house starts to generate, store and sell electricity. Meanwhile, what that electricity costs depends more and more on the clock. Since June 2026, Ireland’s largest suppliers have had to offer tariffs that change every half hour. In the UK, households pay about 26p for each unit they buy, but solar owners can be paid as little as a few pence for each unit they sell.
The question has shifted from how much energy is being used to when is it being consumed? Every building is now an energy system. The clearest example of what that means is a long way from Europe.

In Pakistan, an estimated 7.3 million households, nearly one in five, now have solar panels. In the year to June 2025, panels on homes, shops, farm sheds and small factories produced the equivalent of 46% of all electricity sold through the national grid. Three lessons stand out.

First, nobody paid them to do it. There was no rooftop programme and no subsidy. Squeezed by rising tariffs and power cuts, people bought cheap panels imported from China: nearly 54 gigawatts by March 2026, roughly the capacity of the entire grid.

Second, most of it was invisible. By mid-2025, an estimated 38 gigawatts of solar was installed, generating 51 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to power every home in the UK for more than six months. Yet only 6.8 gigawatts was registered where the regulator could see it. Overall electricity sold through the nation’s grid system fell 11% in three years, and planners could not see what was replacing them.

Third, when the rules caught up, the Pakistani government changed the deal mid-boom. In February 2026, the regulator cut the price paid to new solar customers for exported power by more than two-thirds. After a backlash, those who had already applied kept the old terms. But the households who could never afford panels are left paying for an electricity supply through the nation’s grid infrastructure that fewer people use.

Pakistan is an extreme case, but the direction is global. Electricity is being priced by when it is used, not just how much. In the US, California has paid new solar owners about a quarter of the retail price for exported power since 2023. Australia, which has more midday solar than it can use, now offers households three free hours of electricity at around lunchtime.
The message is the same everywhere. Solar power is worth most when you use it yourself, or when the grid needs it, usually in the early evening.
Measuring when, not just how much

If timing matters this much, we need to measure it. As part of my PhD research, I developed a time-of-use score that rates a home on when it draws power from the grid. Electricity used in the 5pm–7pm peak counts least; electricity used in the after midnight hours, when the grid is quiet, counts most. For homes with solar, a grid interaction score does the same for the power still bought after the panels and batteries have done their work.

We applied the score to newly built, A-rated (highly energy-efficient) apartments that we monitored for a full year. Almost all of them fell into the lowest time-of-use class. On paper these were among the most efficient homes in the country, yet they leaned on the grid at the worst times. Much of their load, such as hot water, washing machines and dishwashers, could easily have moved.
You don’t need a research project to run your solar-fitted home more efficiently as an energy system. Three rules cover most of it.
Use the sun first. Run the dishwasher, washing machine, electric car charger and hot water around midday. A solar diverter can heat your water automatically from surplus power.
Keep off the grid at teatime. Between about 4pm and 7pm, let a battery or a delay timer cover what it can. This is when power is dearest, and the grid is under the most strain.
Buy the rest when it is cheap. In winter, solar may not cover all your needs. Use night or “boost” rates in the small hours to heat water, charge the car and top up the battery.

Then automate. Spain has offered households hourly prices since 2014, yet only 40% of those customers checked the cheapest hours before running big appliances. Timers and smart controls do it every day.

A colleague in our research group took this one step further. Rory Monaghan, a professor in energy systems engineering, wanted to know which electricity supplier and which plan really suited the way his household uses power. So he put his consumption and the available plans into a spreadsheet and ran an optimisation. The results were very different from what you would expect from the suppliers’ adverts. Electricity deals are confusing even for sustainability researchers.

Energy labels across Europe are being redesigned under the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive. This is the moment to rate buildings on how they behave, not just how they were designed: what they use, when they use it, and how they work with the grid.

Pakistan shows what happens when nobody is counting. Millions of buildings can remake an energy system faster than regulators can see it. Better to measure that change, and help every home run itself well, than to discover it from falling grid sales and have to rewrite the rules in a hurry.

articles.title: The worse climate change gets, the harder it becomes to stop it
articles.author: James Dyke, Assistant Director of the Global Systems Institute, University of Exeter
paras: This year may be seen as a turning point in the climate crisis. The UN has accepted that global warming is going to exceed 1.5°C, while climate scientists have concluded that the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade.
What’s worse, the world may be approaching climate tipping points that could trigger further heating and catastrophic environmental change.

Back in 2018, an international team led by Earth system scientist Will Steffen warned that continued greenhouse gas emissions and destruction of biodiversity could produce a cascade of warming that would culminate in the climate systems passing a threshold into a so-called “Hothouse Earth”.

The engine of this cascade would be individual tipping points in the climate. For example, the shutdown of certain Atlantic Ocean currents would not just plunge Europe into freezing winters, but could significantly starve the Amazon rainforest of water vapour. A drought that turns the Amazon to savanna would have huge consequences for the global carbon cycle and climate system. Further warming would accelerate ice sheet loss and ramp up temperatures.

As various tipping points are passed, the Earth system reaches a threshold that could produce a rise in temperatures greater than any for the past 1.2 million years. This would have devastating impacts on ecosystems and societies. Indeed, it’s hard to see how complex, industrialised civilisation would be able to exist in a world that has rapidly warmed beyond 4°C.
Are we responding to the risks?

To what extent the Earth system has the capacity to produce this sort of cascading warming is a topic of intense scientific research. We may be lucky, in that individual tipping elements such as Atlantic current collapse require much higher levels of warming, or more fundamentally the Earth’s current climate may prove to be more resilient than we think. Unfortunately, the opposite may be the case and a planetary threshold may lurk at lower levels of warming than Steffen and colleagues proposed.

It seems reasonable to assume that a deepening climate crisis will focus minds and spur climate action. Unfortunately, new research by my coauthors and I suggests the exact opposite may happen: the worse climate change gets, the harder it could be to stop it. The end point of that process is a disastrous acceleration towards further warming.

Rather than being a purely theoretical exercise, we propose that we can begin to see signs of this slide away from climate action in the real world. For example, those nations most at risk from climate change can be caught in a sovereign debt “doom loop” whereby the damage caused by extreme weather reduces their abilities to repay loans and makes it harder to obtain desperately needed finance to both mitigate and adapt to climate change.

This feedback loop can derail climate policy over time: as debt servicing consumes growing shares of government revenue, climate investments are sidelined, and the country becomes increasingly exposed to climate change.

Increased warming can also increase conflict, thus undermining international cooperation required for mitigation. This is affected by a range of socioeconomic factors, such as inequality and political polarisation.

For example, see the increase in popularity of Spain’s far right-wing and climate-denying Vox party following the devastating Valencia floods of 2024. While the floods were made much more likely because of human-caused climate change, Vox argued that it was left-wing “ideological” environmental policies that made people more vulnerable to the intense rainfall.

The name we give to these dynamics is “derailment risk”, the situation where the consequences of climate change makes it harder to deal with the drivers of climate change, and so sustainability efforts end up being derailed.

Given the potentially devastating consequences of a Hothouse Earth, it seems sensible to minimise the chances of it happening as much as possible. To that end, climate and Earth system scientists have argued that active management of this risk is required.

This “planetary stewardship” goes beyond phasing out the burning of fossil fuels to include strengthening forests, peatlands and other natural stores of carbon, along with behavioural changes, technological innovations, new ways of governing, and transforming social values. But derailment risks could undermine the political and social conditions needed to establish any sort of planetary stewardship.

A key concept here is agency – the capacity to produce change. In the original hothouse framework, agency is essentially one way. Humans affect the Earth system by destabilising it. But humans are not simply an external force acting on the Earth system: we are part of it, and our social and political forces can influence its stability and whether the planet slides into a hothouse state.

We argue that the feedback loops pulling us towards derailment can be stronger than those needed to establish planetary stewardship. That’s because collective action can be easier to destroy than build. At a psychological level, bad events affect people more strongly than good events. This is a factor in how trust within a society can be much easier to undermine than create. Increasing climate change impacts could therefore erode the social institutions needed to sustain effective mitigation and adaptation, just when they are most needed.

To respond to this risk we propose a three-stage framework for assessing and managing derailment threats. First, identify and map feedback loops between the human and natural world; second, anticipate disruption and build resilience; third, develop active responsive governance strategies for periods of escalating instability.

Humans are entirely responsible for the climate and ecological crisis, but we also hold the solutions. Maintaining our agency – the ability to put solutions into practice – may prove to be the keystone for all climate policies.

articles.title: It’s a bumper year for wild mushrooms – here’s what you could find in the woods today
articles.author: Joni Wildman, PhD Candidate in Mycology, University of Bath
paras: This autumn looks like it could be a good year to spot large numbers of wild mushrooms. Already many can be seen covering tree roots and shady spots.

Mushrooms are the part of certain fungi that you see above ground. The rest of it is either underground or within a tree trunk. All mushrooms are part of a fungus, but not all fungi produce mushrooms. There are believed to be 14,000 species of mushroom, and 140,000 of fungi.

To observe what was growing and what wasn’t this autumn, I recently joined a fungi walk in a Somerset woodland. Fungi were everywhere. Our group could barely cover half a kilometre in an hour because there was so much to stop and examine.

Among our sightings were large numbers of bright yellow stagshorn fungi (Calocera viscosa), coral-like clusters emerging from green moss, alongside vivid purple Russulas and more unusual specimens including one looking like a felty black tongue (seen in photo below), which we took for microscopic identification.

Our small group of fungi researchers recorded 39 different fungi. There’s nothing more magical than the iconic red-and-white fly agarics (Amanita muscaria), and our noted observations helped to set a nationwide record for the most of this type recorded in a single day at 276.

Another fungus showing off its colours this year is chicken of the woods (Laetioporus sulphureus). Look out for its cascading, bright yellow lobes bursting from urban trees. Sightings on the citizen science platform iNaturalist of this mushroom have increased by around 25% in the UK, compared with the same period last year.
The mushroom season could be about to get even better. Studies on mushroom production in pine forests have identified rainfall as among the strongest predictors of annual productivity.

Higher temperatures can limit production early in the season but help extend it later. A damp autumn, with enough warmth remaining, could therefore provide excellent mushroom weather. And that is precisely what the UK Met Office is forecasting. With a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific, the chances of a warm, wet autumn in the UK are estimated to be around 1.5 times higher than normal. For fungi emerging from a dry summer, this is good news.

Mushrooms are the temporary fruit that fungi produce for reproduction. The main part of the fungus remains hidden and is a network of tube-like filaments called mycelium, which can come together to form a developing mushroom.
The fungus then has a clever way of using water pressure within its cells to expand this structure and push it above ground, a little like inflating a balloon.
This helps explain why mushrooms often pop up after rain. They need plenty of moisture to grow, and the mushroom “balloon” you see can be up to 90% water.
But more mushrooms don’t always mean healthier ecosystems. An abundance of certain fungi can signal ecosystems under stress.

The long, dry summer has stressed vegetation, potentially leaving trees more vulnerable to pathogens such as honey fungus (Armillaria sp.). These fungi attack living tree roots, sometimes killing their hosts, and produce mushrooms in enormous honey-coloured clusters having done so.
In the dry summer of 2025, the Royal Horticultural Society reported a 43% rise in enquiries about garden fungi, most commonly honey fungus.

Meanwhile, fungi that recycle nutrients by breaking down dead organic matter may have an unusually abundant supply of drought-stricken vegetation to feast on. Another side effect of the very dry summer.

But some species are struggling. Many fungi rely on partnerships with living trees, exchanging nutrients and water for sugars produced through photosynthesis. For these species, vegetation productivity can strongly predict mushroom yield. Drought affecting their host trees may therefore have consequences that autumn rain cannot immediately reverse.

Others need suitable soil conditions to develop their underground mycelium, before producing mushrooms. Some soils in the UK remain exceptionally dry this autumn, requiring substantial rainfall to restore moisture.

Waxcaps, for example, are grassland fungi appearing in extraordinary colours, from pink and yellow to green, with some even smelling of garlic. Associated with long-established, nutrient-poor grasslands, they are valuable indicators of ecological quality.
Prolonged drought could affect their underground mycelium, potentially limiting fruiting even when rain returns. Returning to the balloon analogy, there may simply be nothing to inflate.

October 2026 has seen a 36.6% drop in overall fungi recordings in the UK, compared to October 2025, according to iNaturalist records. However, the season is not yet over, so it’s not yet clear how things will pan out.

To observe the latest growth, head to your local woodland or grassland, pick up a field guide or join a guided walk. You don’t need to identify everything to appreciate it, and while no UK mushrooms are dangerous to touch, never eat one unless you’re absolutely certain of its identity.

This autumn’s abundance may have prompted some commercial pickers to sweep through woods picking large numbers of fungi. The Woodland Trust, a charity, has warned this can put wildlife under pressure as they are a source of food for animals such as deer and support the soil’s health. While foraging for personal use is allowed, picking for commercial sale is illegal.
By recording your finds through citizen science projects such as iNaturalist, you can also help experts understand which species are flourishing and which are struggling in a changing climate.
If the forecast threatens your outdoor plans this autumn, remember what might soon be popping up after the rain. This might just be the year you discover some remarkable mushrooms for yourself.

articles.title: Imagine newsletter: the power of plankton
articles.author: Anna Turns, Senior Environment Editor, The Conversation
paras: This roundup of The Conversation’s environment coverage was first published in our award-winning weekly climate action newsletter, Imagine.
In a world without plankton, I wouldn’t get stung by jellyfish when swimming in the sea. But my friend’s fish and chip shop would go bust. There’d be big climate implications too.

Plankton, meaning “drifter” in Greek, encompasses all the viruses, bacteria, insects, larval fish and jellyfish that don’t actively swim. Instead, they drift in oceans, rivers and lakes, at the whim of currents and tides. Many are microscopic; some, like barrel jellyfish, are huge.
I recently explored the planet’s reliance on plankton in a new episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Without series with TV presenter and comedian Alan Davies. Listen to this thought experiment here.

Don’t have time to read about climate change as much as you’d like? Get a weekly roundup in your inbox instead. Every Wednesday, The Conversation’s environment editor writes Imagine, a short email that goes a little deeper into just one climate issue. Join the 50,000+ readers who’ve subscribed so far.

First, a quick food web refresher. Algal plankton or phytoplankton are single-celled organisms that photosynthesise to produce oxygen and capture carbon dioxide. These form the base of the marine food web. Next up, it’s zooplankton, tiny marine animals that feed on phytoplankton. Without zooplankton like copepods (a microscopic crustacean), young fish, basking sharks and blue whales wouldn’t have anything to eat. When those animals die and sink, so too does the carbon captured during photosynthesis, so phytoplankton are an essential climate variable.

Climate change increases the frequency of marine heatwaves and the distribution of some plankton is already shifting towards the poles where ocean temperatures are cooler. By looking at the fossil record of plankton, researchers have found that some plankton are now less able to adapt to climate change than they were in the past.

Geological warming around the last ice age 21,000 years ago was relatively gradual. A study by paleobiologists at the University of Bristol found that “current climate change is too rapid and is reducing food supply … making plankton difficult to adapt to this time”.

Depending on their location, phytoplankton’s chemical fingerprint varies. So much so, that crime scene investigators can diagnose drowning in a specific location depending on the presence of certain microscopic plankton.

This “postcode” also gets transferred to other animals as they feed on these ocean drifters. Plankton postcodes have helped a global team of marine biologists map the feeding habits of 114 different species of sharks.

Christopher Bird and Clive Trueman at the University of Southampton found that sharks living in coastal waters, such as the great white or reef sharks, had been feeding close to where they were caught. Sharks in the open ocean, such as mako sharks, appeared to get most of their food from a specific plankton postcode, no matter where in the world they were caught. And knowing where sharks feed helps protect them.
Plankton help control the formation of clouds over remote seas in the Southern Ocean far from land.

“Clouds are made up of many tiny droplets of water that have condensed from water vapour onto microscopic particles floating in the Earth’s atmosphere. These particles are known as cloud condensation nuclei. Plankton essentially help provide clouds with these nuclei to form around,” says Daniel Grosvenor, a researcher at the University of Leeds.

His team found that more cloud droplets tended to occur above patches of the ocean with more plankton. Plankton could influence cloud albedo (the amount of energy from the Sun that’s reflected back to space). Grosvenor’s study also suggests that, in a lifeless ocean without phytoplankton, the Southern Ocean’s surface would probably be “somewhat warmer”.

articles.title: From doctors and teachers to lawyers, every profession has a duty to align with climate goals
articles.author: Aaron Thierry, PhD Candidate, Social Science, Cardiff University
paras: A Dutch family doctor called Tibor Poelmann posted a petition on an online forum for GPs in 2021. He wanted their pension fund to stop investing in oil and gas. It quickly gathered 1,200 signatures.

Three years later the fund, which looks after €10 billion (£8.4 billion) for 25,000 doctors, decided to sell all its fossil fuel investments. The push came from the doctors themselves, through a council of GPs elected by the fund’s members.

Our new paper in the journal Frontiers in Education was inspired by cases like this. Research on who can act on climate change tends to sort the world into governments, markets and campaigners. Professionals fall between those groups. We treat them as a class of climate changemaker with their own means of influence.

Nearly everyone agrees something has to be done, yet on current policies the world is still heading for nearly 3°C of warming. Responsibility is scattered across governments, businesses and individuals, each able to point to someone else who should act first. Psychologists call this diffusion of responsibility. In everyday life, that sounds like “that’s not my job”.

A doctor’s focus is health, a lawyer’s is the rule of law, an engineer’s is structures that stand up and a teacher’s is the children in front of them. Climate change now threatens each of those. Doctors owe duties to patients, and lawyers to clients. Climate change has begun to harm those people, so acting on climate change as part of doing the job well.

Professionals also influence the institutions and decisions that shape how society responds. Doctors decide what gets prescribed and sit on the bodies that write clinical guidance. Lawyers advise the companies whose projects need permission. Engineers build to standards their own institution sets.

Each works inside an institution that needs to change and belongs to a profession that can rewrite its own rules. Health professionals also rank among the most trusted messengers on climate, whatever the listener’s politics. Governments still have to act, and professions are among the things that drive political change. It was doctors who turned smoking from a habit into a health problem, then the laws followed.

Yet professional authority can stall action too. Training instils standards and ethics, so that a patient or client can rely on the result, but those same standards and routines can make established ways of working difficult to challenge.

Without a push, professionals keep running the systems that cause the harm, competently and by the book. Healthcare has increased its greenhouse gas emissions by a quarter since 2016. Top American law schools send graduates into the oil and gas industry at well above the national rate. One student campaign calls this the fossil fuel lawyer pipeline. Teacher training, if it covers climate at all, teaches the science of a warming planet and says little about its social and economic causes.
How can a profession begin to change? Our paper identifies three stages at which climate responsibility can become part of professional practice.

First, the profession needs to recognise climate change in its own terms. In medicine that has happened, with more than 200 medical journals jointly calling climate change the greatest threat to global public health. In law it is happening through pledges like Lawyers Are Responsible, whose signatories refuse work that undermines the 1.5°C warming limit agreed by the UN. Teachers can see how climate change undermines children’s learning, as hot classrooms sap concentration plus storms and wildfires close schools.

Second, recognition turns into duty, because it won’t automatically trigger action. The clearest case so far is in law. The Law Society, which represents solicitors in England and Wales, now tells them they have a duty to warn clients about climate risk, and advice that ignores climate looks less and less like competent advice.

Third, the duty is written into the rules and institutions a profession controls, from its codes of conduct and accreditation standards to its pension fund. This is where individual concern can become collective professional practice. That is what the Dutch GPs’ elected council did when it made divestment the fund’s policy. In Canada, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons is writing planetary health, the idea that human health depends on the planet’s health, into the framework that defines a competent Canadian doctor.
Where professions get stuck

Most professions have stalled before the third stage. Medicine has called climate change its greatest threat for years. Yet a student-run audit of 188 health schools in 21 countries, the Planetary Health Report Card, still finds many teaching little about it. Most bar associations have yet to say whether helping to expand fossil fuel production raises any ethical question.

The same questions extend beyond medicine, law and education. Engineers, accountants, planners, social workers and police officers all work under their own codes, regulators and training requirements. Climate change threatens what each profession is there to protect. A few have started to write it into their rules.

Canada’s government has set a target that by 2027, 70% of its engineers, planners, accountants and landscape architects should be able to help clients adapt to climate change. Adapting means preparing for the heat, floods and wildfires that are already here, whatever happens to emissions. Professions Advancing Adaptation Competencies is writing those skills into each profession’s standards.

If you belong to a professional body, ask it three questions. Does its code of conduct mention climate change? Does the training you need to stay qualified cover it? Where is your pension invested? If the answers are no, no and don’t know, our paper sets out how your profession could change them.

articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.author: Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California
paras: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally.

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record.
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.
Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%.
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high.
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978.

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs.
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon.
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon.

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon.

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels.

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.
As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war.

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

articles.title: Short supplies of crucial equipment stymie changes to US electricity grid
articles.author: Jasmine Garland, Chancellors Postdoctoral Fellow in Civil, Environmental and Architectural Engineering, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: Americans have a lot of plans for the country’s power grid. Some people want to expand renewable energy by building solar and wind farms. Others want to add new coal- or natural gas-fired power plants. There are those who want to provide power to some unknown number of data centers processing artificial intelligence algorithms.

To accomplish any of these goals, the country will need a significant number of pieces of equipment whose design was invented in the late 19th century: large power transformers. These giant metal structures are about the size of a two-story house and weigh as much as 400 tons – roughly equivalent to a fully loaded Boeing 747. They convert high voltages used to transmit electricity down to voltage levels people can use in their homes and businesses. And they are made largely in the same way they were when they were invented 150 years ago.

Many of the large power transformers in service in the U.S. and around the world are aging beyond their intended lifespans. And there aren’t enough replacements to meet the world’s needs. It can take more than three years for a company’s order to be filled and delivered.
Transformers as transport systems

Large power transformers are crucial to transporting electricity over long distances. Power plants – whether coal- or gas-fired, hydropower dams, or solar or wind farms – are often far from the customers who need the electricity that’s generated.

Transmitting power through wires generates heat, which over a long distance dramatically reduces the amount of energy arriving at the far end. To reduce energy losses, power companies use large transformers to increase the voltage. You can think of this like freight being loaded onto large trucks and directed over interstate highways. They can carry a lot of energy more efficiently than smaller cars could on smaller roads.

But the high-voltage power is not safe for a home or business to use right away, just as a semitruck at highway speeds shouldn’t try to enter your driveway. So when the power arrives near a group of customers, it needs to take an off-ramp, going through another large transformer that lowers its voltage to levels regular customers can use. Then low-voltage lines act as local city streets, delivering the electricity the short distance from the highway exit to homes and businesses.

Between 2019 and 2025, demand for generator step-up transformers, those that connect power plants to the transmission grid, nearly tripled. And over the same period, demand for transformers to work as off-ramps more than doubled, with costs increasing 80%.

These devices are not mass-produced from automated assembly lines. They are custom-engineered to meet specific needs and demands for their intended destinations. If a specialized transformer fails during an extreme storm or heat wave, there aren’t just replacements waiting in a warehouse somewhere.
What these transformers are made of is a big part of the delay.

One key ingredient is what’s known as grain-oriented electrical steel. This is not at all average steel. It is manufactured using precise thermal and mechanical processes that position the steel’s magnetic crystals in a single direction. The crystalline alignment allows magnetic fields to pass through the metal with low energy loss, which is crucial for handling large amounts of electricity. However, only a handful of specialized steel mills worldwide have the technology to produce it. Just one mill is in the U.S.
Also in short supply is copper, which is made into wires that are wrapped around the core of the transformer, typically made of steel, to achieve the correct voltage adjustment.
Work-around has its own problems

Because of the transformer shortage, it can take utilities and power producers more than two years to get equipment to connect new power plants to the grid – regardless of whether they are powered by nuclear energy, fossil fuels, solar energy or the wind.

To get around that delay, companies that run data centers to power artificial intelligence systems have sought to bypass the grid altogether, by installing dedicated, on-site natural gas power plants to run the computer centers.

That move has caused another supply chain problem. Gas turbines burn at over 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,100 C), which is hot enough to melt standard steel. Turbine blades are manufactured with a complicated process out of very specialized combinations of metal and coated with ceramic heat shields.

As tech companies have placed more and larger orders, the time between ordering a gas turbine and having it delivered has stretched to between three and seven years. And prices in 2027 are expected to be nearly triple what they were in 2019, due to the increase in demand and still-rare materials.
A supply chain built in the 19th century is struggling to reliably serve power to the 21st-century economy.
Large power transformers are also key to upgrading the existing grid and reducing its vulnerability to large storms or extended outages.
The solutions are both concrete and complicated.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has recommended standardizing transformer designs, rather than having each be custom-built. That would allow manufacturers to produce more units more quickly, with an assembly line-style process. It would also allow utility companies to share emergency spares.

The U.S. Department of Energy has recommended deploying what are collectively called “grid-enhancing technologies.” These methods include sensors that monitor in real time exactly how much power can be transmitted through long-distance wires and advanced software that can find alternative routes by which to distribute electricity from power plants to maximize what’s available to customers. Together, these types of systems can allow the transmission of 15% to 20% more electricity than without them, easing bottlenecks while waiting for new transformers to be delivered.
Longer term, the U.S. could produce more grain-oriented electrical steel, process more copper and expand its capacity to build large power transformers.
All the ways people want to adapt, improve, expand and modernize the power grid are dependent on this one type of equipment. Without large power transformers, none of the efforts will get very far.

In a sense, leaders face a choice either way: solve these hardware shortages or accept the default consequences of grid congestion, delayed projects and rising costs. Resolving the transformer bottleneck would be what turns that passive reality into active choice.

articles.title: Fireworks provide a few minutes of joy, but the economic and environmental costs last much longer
articles.author: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter
paras: Every Bonfire Night, people pay for a box of fireworks so their friends and family can enjoy the colourful display. Within a few minutes, it’s all over. But the price on the box doesn’t reflect the hidden costs. The smoke inhaled by neighbours, the animals disturbed or the public services called out when things go wrong.

It’s not a question about whether fireworks celebrations are enjoyable, but whether the people enjoying them are aware of – or actually paying for – their full cost. Economists call this a “negative externality”. A purchase benefits the buyer and seller, but some of its costs fall on people outside that transaction. Fireworks offer a particularly visible example because the enjoyment is concentrated in time while the consequences are spread among households, public services and wildlife. As a finance researcher, I think this concept is overlooked in the fireworks debate.

Consider injuries. Figures show that 123 hospital admissions in England attributed to fireworks in 2024–25. That is not a count of everyone injured: cases treated without hospital admission are excluded. Preventing such injuries may not cut the NHS budget, but it can free clinical time for other patients. In an overstretched health service, that is an economic benefit even if it never appears as a saving in the Treasury’s accounts.

Pollution creates another unpriced cost. The UK’s official air-quality monitoring has recorded short-lived spikes in fine particles around Bonfire Night, although bonfires also contribute and weather affects how quickly smoke disperses. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs assigns a central estimated damage cost of £114,411 per tonne of fine particulate emissions (known as PM2.5), expressed in 2025 prices to account for inflation. This is not a figure for fireworks: calculating that would require information about their emissions and who is exposed. It does show why a product can have an environmental cost that never appears on its receipt.
Nature belongs on the balance sheet

The damage is not limited to human health. In a peer-reviewed Dutch study, researchers found that approximately 1,000 times as many birds were flying during New Year’s Eve fireworks as on ordinary nights. The disruption extended several miles from the displays. The exact scale cannot be transferred to British Bonfire Nights, but the finding challenges the idea that fireworks affect only those who choose to watch.

Birds forced into sudden flight expend energy and lose opportunities to rest. Pets and livestock may also be distressed. Alongside noise and smoke, spent casings and other waste leave a physical footprint. Sustainability means considering these effects, not simply asking how much carbon a celebration emits.

Yet putting nature on an economic balance sheet requires care. The value of healthy ecosystems is real, but we should not invent a monetary figure for fireworks-related wildlife damage when credible national estimates are lacking. Some effects can be quantified; others must still inform decisions even without an exact price.

Fireworks also create value. They support retailers, display organisers and cultural celebrations, including Bonfire Night, Diwali and New Year. The UK government’s 2026 consultation reports that fireworks imports averaged £27 million a year from 2021 to 2024. That is the value of imports, not total industry sales and certainly not what Britain would save by banning them.

If households bought fewer fireworks, they might spend on a local community event, food or another kind of entertainment instead. They might equally save the money. There is no basis for promising that fewer fireworks would automatically increase jobs, GDP or tax receipts.

But GDP and wellbeing are not the same thing. Treating avoidable injuries and clearing pollution may involve paid work without making society better off. The relevant comparison is between the enjoyment fireworks provide and the harm, resources and opportunities their use consumes.

The practical question is not simply whether to completely ban fireworks and take the joy out of Bonfire Night. It makes more sense to ask which forms of celebration produce the most enjoyment with the least harm. Organised displays, fewer private launches, predictable timings and wildlife-sensitive locations could change that balance. Drone and laser shows might offer alternatives, but they also require electricity and equipment; their sustainability should be assessed, not assumed.

This is especially timely. The government’s fireworks consultation closed in October 2026 after receiving more than 140,000 responses from members of the public, businesses, charities and other stakeholders.

Policymakers now have an opportunity to assess the social costs alongside safety, business impacts and cultural value. A credible assessment would be honest about what the evidence shows, and about the nationwide economic savings that cannot yet be calculated. Because when a fireworks celebration leaves a bill for people who never attended, its market price only tells part of the story.

articles.title: US wildfire damage is on pace to triple by mid-century, but there are affordable ways to lower the risk
articles.author: Virginia Iglesias, Earth Lab Director, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.S. is on pace to triple by mid-century, my colleagues and I found in a study just published.

The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire don’t have to be overly expensive.
The 2026 western fire season

The 2026 wildfire season began with historically low mountain snowpack, early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s hottest summer on record intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out.

Colorado’s Aspen Acres Fire destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving Knowles Fire overtook them near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in Spokane, Washington, damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate.

In Colorado, the summer monsoon season brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures.

Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had burned more than 318,000 acres by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also well above average. The U.S. spent 48 consecutive days at Preparedness Level 5 – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a 10-year average of 25 days annually.
Reasons for rising fire risk

Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a century of fire suppression has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned.

Rising temperatures caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying nearly doubled the area burned in western U.S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change.

More people also now live in and at the edges of wildland areas, raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round.
These interacting factors have helped nearly quadruple the annual area burned in the western United States since 2000.
They also contribute to the growing threat of fast-growing fires, which can overwhelm emergency response.

In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2.7% of fires analyzed but accounted for 78% of documented structures destroyed and 61% of reported firefighting costs.

A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster.
The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U.S., raising the risk of damage.

Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk expanded tenfold, increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building.

My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean up to 449,000 structures lost between 2026 and 2060.

We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations.

We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities. In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire.
How to lower your wildfire risk
These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now.

For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with Class A fire-resistant roofs and ember-resistant vents that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. Removing flammable debris, mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. Community programs are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk.

Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the Colorado fire code increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0.6% and 4.2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable.
Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it.

Beyond individual buildings, prescribed burning and appropriately designed forest-thinning operations can reduce fuels and alter fire behavior before flames reach neighborhoods. Utilities can strengthen infrastructure and reduce the probability of ignition while limiting disruptions from preventive power shut-offs. Insurance companies can reward measurable risk reduction and help sustain coverage in communities working to become safer.

These measures work best when they reinforce one another. The odds of losing a home to wildfire depend on its construction, its immediate surroundings and the broader neighborhood. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to wildfire risk. As the threat grows, strategies tailored to the environmental, social and economic realities of each community are more important than ever.
Virginia Iglesias receives funding from the National Science Foundation and from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety

articles.title: The world promised to halt biodiversity loss by 2030 – now it needs to turn pledges into action
articles.author: Gabriella Santini, Post-doctoral Researcher in Anthropology, UCL
paras: The UN’s main biodiversity summit, held every two years, wrapped up in Yerevan, Armenia, on October 31.

Biodiversity summits don’t attract the same fanfare as their climate change equivalents, yet loss of nature threatens food systems, water security, health, livelihoods and cultural traditions. Forests, soils, wetlands and oceans absorb around half the carbon dioxide humans emit, while climate change is itself one of the main drivers of biodiversity loss.

This summit, technically the 17th Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) conference, or Cop17, was meant to take stock of progress and accelerate action on protecting biodiversity. Back in 2022, the same conference launched an ambitious framework to reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, a goal that will require closing an US$700 billion (£520 billion) per year finance gap.

Targets include protecting 30% of land and sea, restoring degraded ecosystems, and halting the extinction of threatened species. Yerevan was the halfway point, and the first time countries formally reviewed how they were doing.

The first global review of the framework, State of Biodiversity Action, showed how little progress has been made. Almost 90% of countries have set national targets, but fewer than half are on track. The targets lagging furthest behind – covering business impacts, unsustainable consumption, harmful subsidies and finance – are the ones that need action beyond environment ministries and conservation programmes.

It comes down to money: who should pay for biodiversity protection? The framework calls for US$200 billion a year from all sources by 2030, including US$30 billion per year through international finance.

Two debates stood out. The first concerned who should manage the funds. Lower-income countries have argued for a new funding mechanism under the CBD’s control. Many high-income countries prefer the current Global Environment Facility, which critics say is bureaucratic and hard for local communities to access. Decisions on a new financial mechanism have been pushed to the next summit, Cop18, in Ecuador in 2028.

The second debate was about extending the list of countries expected to provide finance to developing countries. Emerging economies such as Saudi Arabia and Qatar resisted, as it would shift their contributions from voluntary to obligatory. In the end, it was agreed that countries that now want to contribute as donors can “signal interest” before Cop18.

The summit presidency announced that more than US$1.8 billion had been pledged from governments, philanthropic organisations and investors. That is welcome, but negligible compared with what is needed. Recent cuts to development aid have made the shortfall even harder to address.

The negotiations looked at alternative ways of valuing nature, such as natural capital accounting or treating nature as infrastructure. “Biodiversity is not just for tree-huggers,” said the CBD’s executive secretary Astrid Schomaker at a workshop in Yerevan, suggesting it should matter to business.
Cutting or redirecting US$500 billion a year in harmful subsidies would help fund all this. But though this is the framework’s target 18, little progress has been made.
Who benefits from genetic data?

So-called digital sequence information, or DSI, was another subject of contention. This is genetic data gathered from plants, animals and microbes, stored in online databases and used by companies to develop medicines, crops and cosmetics. However, the countries and communities where these organisms come from have rarely been paid for their use.

The 2024 biodiversity summit in Colombia created the Cali Fund to change this. Large companies using DSI are expected to pay 1% of their profits or 0.1% of their revenue to this fund. At least half of the money is meant to go to Indigenous peoples and local communities.
The fund was expected to raise at least US$1 billion a year. By the end of this year’s summit, just five companies had committed a total of just US$10,565.

Part of the problem is that contributions are voluntary. Negotiators debated who counts as a user of DSI, whether only large companies should pay, and how to avoid companies being charged twice under national and international schemes. After fraught discussions and delays, many of the key decisions were postponed to the next summit in 2028.
The role of Indigenous people
Indigenous peoples and local communities manage or hold rights over a large share of the world’s remaining biodiverse land. In 2024, parties created a permanent body to strengthen their role.

In Yerevan, discussions focused on how it should work: who leads it, and who chooses the representatives. Campaigners warned that governments were deciding how Indigenous peoples should be represented instead of letting them decide for themselves. In the 12-hour-long final plenary, the body’s rules of operation were agreed, but as an advisory body, its influence will depend on whether governments listen.

Women’s rights were another focus. The global progress review found that only about a quarter of countries’ national targets address women’s land rights or access, leaving women with little power in conservation decisions. The Yerevan summit encouraged governments to embed gender equity into national biodiversity strategies and data collection.
Finance, DSI and Indigenous rights may have been separate items on the agenda, but they raise the same questions: who pays to protect nature, who gets to decide, and who benefits?

The agreed Yerevan Pathway urges countries to take faster action on priorities including cutting subsidies that harm nature, providing financial and technical support to developing countries, and aligning national budgets with biodiversity goals. But it leans heavily on commitments already made.

Outside the main negotiations in Yerevan, Indigenous groups, campaigners and non-governmental organisations showcased their work protecting and restoring nature in spite of limited funding. The tension between biodiversity targets and the extractive industries was also visible in protests against a controversial gold mine, which recently began production in south-eastern Armenia.

Governments now need to back their commitments with money that reaches the people doing the work, an end to economic incentives that drive nature loss, and a meaningful say for Indigenous people and local communities.
